title: Your Evals Are Meaningless (And Here’s How to Fix Them)
talk_summary: The speaker argues that LLM-as-judge evals silently fail through 'criteria drift' (generic templated metrics that don't match your product's notion of good) and 'dataset drift' (test sets that don't reflect real user inputs), and prescribes iteratively aligning evaluator prompts and test banks against domain-expert judgment, measured with F1/correlation over time. The core mechanism is a feedback loop: log production failures, promote them into the test bank, tune the judge prompt with expert few-shot critiques, and track judge-human agreement.

takeaways.technique: Custom judge prompt instead of templated metrics
takeaways.what_they_do: They reject out-of-the-box framework metrics (RAGAS, promptfoo, LangChain) because those are built for generalizability, and instead hand-tune the evaluator prompt with few-shot examples of expert critiques so the judge measures what the business actually cares about.
takeaways.evidence_quote: their evaluation criteria is designed for generalizability it doesn't necessarily measure what's important to your unique use case

takeaways.technique: Promote production failures into the test bank
takeaways.what_they_do: Every time the system underperforms in production, that case is logged and added to the test set with ground-truth labels, so the eval suite grows from real failures instead of hand-written happy-path cases.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every time your system underperforms in production that's an opportunity to improve your test Bank

takeaways.technique: Measure judge-human agreement (F1) before trusting a cheaper judge
takeaways.what_they_do: They track alignment between LLM-judge verdicts and human/domain-expert verdicts with F1 for binary judgments (or correlation for Likert), and recommend binary scales over Likert, so you know whether a judge is actually improving or regressing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use conrete metrics like F1 score for binary judgments or correlation coefficients for liard scales track how well your evaluator matches human judgment
takeaways.numbers: ~80% consistency with human judgments cited for LLM judges; human-human agreement is similar

takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly recommend binary judgments for evaluators rather than 1-5 scales, because binary is easier to align and to measure with F1.
takeaways.evidence_quote: pay attention to whether you're actually using binary skilles or lard skills for Ratings highly recommend binary by the way

takeaways.technique: Pin judge model version to stop criteria drift
takeaways.what_they_do: They cite a case where an evaluator stopped grading consistently because the underlying model silently changed; the fix is using a stable/pinned model version for the judge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they weren't using a stable version of open AI so this is what we consider criteria drift

takeaways.what_they_do: They suggest starting alignment with as few as 20 examples graded by a domain expert in a spreadsheet to see whether judge verdicts match expert judgment before investing in tooling.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can start with even like 20 examples and it will give you a good sense of whether evaluated judgments are actually in line with your demain experts
